rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Electrical work W = qV becomes power $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$ (watt). Choose the form by what's common: in series compare I²R (bigger resistor dissipates more); in parallel compare V²/R (smaller resistor wins). Joule heating $H = I^2Rt$ converts electrical energy to heat — toasters by design, transmission losses by accident (hence high-voltage grids).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - P = VI = I²R = V²/R - H = I²Rt (Joule's law of heating) - 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Power Formula Context:** $P = I^2R$ is used when current is known (series circuits). $P = V^2/R$ is used when voltage is known (parallel circuits). Both are derived from $P = VI$ and Ohm's law; using the wrong one gives incorrect results because $V$ and $I$ are coupled through $R$.  ·  **Joule Heating is Irreversible:** The power $P = I^2R$ dissipated in a resistor represents an irreversible conversion of electrical energy to heat. It cannot be recovered within the circuit. This is distinct from energy stored in inductors/capacitors or converted to mechanical work.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is converted: P = VI."

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Series → compare with I²R; parallel → compare with V²/R** — pick the formula whose variable is common.  ·  **1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J** — the meter's unit, not a power.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Watts in the Wire Every appliance is a bargain between voltage, current and power. P = VI and its two disguises — I²R and V²/R — decide the bill, the fuse, the brightness and the burn. Electrical heating is the same physics with intent.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Work, power and the three formulas Moving charge q through potential difference V does work W = qV. Power is the rate: $$P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R} \qquad W = VIt \qquad \text{unit: watt (W) = J/s}$$ - **Series circuit:** same I everywhere → compare power with I²R (the larger resistor dissipates more).…

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A 220 V, 60 W bulb: find I and hot resistance.** — I = 60/220 ≈ 0.27 A; R = 220²/60 ≈ 807 Ω.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Choose the comparison formula by what's common in the circuit.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Joule heating is unavoidable dissipation** — every real current pays I²R.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: P = VI = I²R = V²/R; H = I²Rt; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Grids transmit at hundreds of kV because P_loss = I²R shrinks as I falls for the same delivered power.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Power formulas and when each is the honest comparison** | Formula | Best when | Series example | Parallel example | |---|---|---|---| | $P = VI$ | always valid | — | — | | $P = I²R$ | same I (series) | bigger R wins | misleading | | $P = V²/R$ | same V (parallel) | misleading | smaller R wins | | Energy | $W = Pt = VIt$ | 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ | — |  ·  **Everyday power ratings (NEB context)** | Appliance | Power | Energy in 1 h | |---|---|---| | LED bulb | 9 W | 9 Wh | | Filament bulb | 60 W | 60 Wh | | Fan | 75 W | 75 Wh | | Heater | 1500 W | 1.5 kWh | | 1 unit (kWh) | 1000 W for 1 h | 3.6 MJ |  ·  ### Deep dive: one watt, three formulas — pick by what is shared Electrical work is $W = VIt$ and power $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$; the three forms are algebraically identical *only* when you know which quantity is common to the elements. In series, the same I flows, so comparing $I^2R$ is honest — the larger R dissipates more.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Energy Units:** Electrical energy is measured in joules (SI) or kilowatt-hours (practical). $1 ext{ kWh} = 3.6 imes 10^6 ext{ J}$. Power (watts) is the *rate* of energy transfer, not energy itself.  ·  No verified PYQ; NEB-style practice (formulas 3m, ratings 2–3m).  ·  Why do kettles need thick short elements while transmission lines want thin long ones... or do they?
